title: Your AI Agent Is One Prompt Injection Away From Spending Your Credentials — Here’s How an Apigee Gateway Stops It
summary: Discover how an Apigee gateway acts as an airlock for AI agents, preventing prompt injection, masking PII, and securing credentials.
body_markdown:
## **Key takeaways**


- Enforce security at the gateway layer. An agent is only as trustworthy as the least trustworthy text it reads, so scope its requests, not its instructions.
- Credentials belong in the gateway, not the agent. The blast radius of a fully compromised agent should be dictated by a policy decision, not a token’s scope. Store tokens in Apigee’s encrypted KVM so agent processes never hold spendable backend secrets.
- Put the model call behind the same identity, quota, and audit as the tools, and a session becomes one story in one log. Route LLM traffic through Apigee to apply identity, rate limits, and response redaction across tool and reasoning planes.
- Audit all refusals. Log every denied action to maintain complete visibility into what agents attempt to do.


### If you’re running AI agents today, there’s a good chance one of them is holding a GitHub token, a Slack bot token, or a model provider key in plain environment variables — right inside the very process that reads untrusted text all day. With one well-crafted prompt injection, an attacker can do everything that token can do.


If you’re a platform and DevOps engineer who puts Large Language Model (LLM) agents into real workflows, you likely find yourself asking uncomfortable questions:


- “Who can see what the agent did?”
- “What happens when it loops?”
- “What exactly can it spend and on whose behalf?”


The short answer to these questions is to treat the agent like an untrusted client. Put an Application Programming Interface (API) gateway between it and everything it touches — its tools *and* its model — then let the gateway own the credentials, the limits, and the audit trail.


This post features a custom-built, working example of this pattern deployed on Google Cloud’s Apigee, walking through seven concrete challenges of agentic workflows. Real snapshots from the deployed gateway will illustrate how each challenge is countered.


The price of the entire stack — identity checks, quotas, payload screening, credential injection, redaction, and a full audit trail — is about **90–100 milliseconds per request** , proving that security is not what makes an agent slow.


The full example is open source and can be replicated on an Apigee evaluation organization in a single afternoon.


## Why agents break the usual security model


A conventional service holds a credential and uses it exactly the way its code dictates. An agent is different in one crucial way: its “code” is partly model-generated text, which can be steered by anything the model reads. This includes things like an issue body, a web page, or a document it was asked to summarize. The industry calls this “prompt injection,” and it means an agent is exactly as trustworthy as the least trustworthy content that enters its context.


That reality has a hard consequence: If the agent’s process holds a real backend credential, a successful injection can spend the entire thing. Scoping the agent’s instructions doesn’t help. Instead, you need to scope what its requests can physically do. That is a gateway’s job.


## A working example: The agent airlock


This working example — what I call the “agent airlock” — is a set of Apigee proxies and shared flows that sit in front of three backends: GitHub issues, Slack messages, and an OpenAI-compatible model plane backed by OpenRouter. Two primary components talk to it:


- A **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** server: MCP is the emerging standard for connecting agents to tools. This runs locally next to the agent and holds *no backend credentials* . Every tool call leaves the machine as an ordinary Hyper Text Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) request to Apigee, authenticated with a single gateway consumer key.
- Two **Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)** agents: Their model calls go through the same gateway using the same key. The reasoning half of the session is governed by the exact same airlock as the acting half.


Every request passes through the same chain: verify the key, check what that identity is allowed to do, rate-limit it, screen the payload, inject the real backend credential from an encrypted Key Value Map (KVM, Apigee’s encrypted store), call the backend, redact the response, and write an audit record. The agent never sees a real credential in either direction.


Detailed architecture and traffic flow can be found[here](https://github.com/farooq-kahout-insight/apigee-mcp-gateway) .


*Legend: ALB = Application Load Balancer · NEG = Network Endpoint Group · PSC = Private Service Connect · VPC = Virtual Private Cloud · HTTPS = Hyper Text Transfer Protocol Secure · URL = Uniform Resource Locator*


Based on this deployment, here are the seven critical challenges an agent faces. Each section below outlines the problem, explains the architectural counter, and provides a snapshot from the live gateway:


- **Challenge 1** — The agent holds credentials it can leak.
- **Challenge 2** — Every agent is as powerful as its most powerful tool.
- **Challenge 3** — A prompt injection can spend legitimate access anywhere.
- **Challenge 4** — Agents loop, and loops cost money.
- **Challenge 5** — The model call is the one request that bypasses all supervision.
- **Challenge 6** — Whatever enters the agent’s context will eventually leave it.
- **Challenge 7** — You can’t govern what you can’t see.


## Challenge 1: The agent holds credentials it can leak.


**The problem:** The standard MCP server setup hands the server a GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) or a Slack bot token via environment variables. From that moment, the agent’s process is exactly as privileged as that token. A prompt injection, a stack trace, a debug log, or a compromised dependency can exfiltrate it. A Slack bot token in particular is painful because it can’t be scoped to specific channels.


**The counter:** In this deployment, backend credentials exist in exactly one place: an encrypted KVM inside Apigee. The PAT, the Slack token, and the OpenRouter key are injected into the request inside the gateway’s target endpoint microseconds before the upstream socket opens. The agent’s side of the wire holds only an Apigee consumer key, which is meaningless anywhere except this gateway. It is scoped to a handful of operations, rate-limited, and revocable in one API call without requiring you to rotate the real credential.


The example goes one step further: The MCP server refuses to start if it finds` GITHUB_TOKEN` ,` SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` , a webhook URL, or any of a dozen other credential-shaped variables in its environment.


*All credentials and allowlists are stored in the Apigee KVM.*


## Challenge 2: Every agent is as powerful as its most powerful tool.


**The problem:** Most agent setups feature one identity with one set of tools. The agent summarizing issues holds the exact same authority as the agent creating them. Least privilege — the oldest idea in security — tends to disappear the moment an agent framework enters the picture.


**The counter:** Apigee’s API Products make identity the unit of authority. The example runs the same codebase under two distinct identities:


- ` agent-reader` can read weather, list issues, and read Slack history.
- ` agent-operator` can additionally create issues and post messages.


The scope check happens inside Apigee, before any proxy logic runs. No prompt, tool description, or injected instruction can turn the reader’s key into one that can write. The refusal is a strict fact about the credential, not the request.


The policy driving this is incredibly lightweight; the authority lives in the API Product the key resolves to, not in proxy code:


```text
<VerifyAPIKey continueOnError="false" enabled="true" name="VA-VerifyAPIKey">
<DisplayName>VA-VerifyAPIKey</DisplayName>
<APIKey ref="request.header.x-api-key"/>
</VerifyAPIKey>


```


*An agent can do what its identity is allowed to do.*


*An agent with appropriate permissions can both read and create issues.*


## Challenge 3: A prompt injection can spend legitimate access anywhere.


**The problem:** Even a correctly scoped write is dangerous if the destination is attacker-chosen. A Slack token with` chat:write` can post to every channel the bot is` in` , exposing roughly 200 methods behind one token via the Slack Web API. A GitHub PAT for “create issues” can create them on any repository it reaches, and an issue’s` assignees` field can page a human being.


**The counter:** This is addressed by three independent controls, none of which substitutes for another.


1. **Resource allowlists.** The gateway will spend the PAT on exactly one named repository and the Slack token on explicitly listed channel IDs. These are enforced by KVM lookups that fail *closed* : An unprovisioned allowlist denies everything. Refusals deliberately do not echo the requested target, ensuring the error can’t be used to probe what exists.
2. **Payload rebuilding.** The gateway doesn’t sanitize the issue body. Instead, it discards it and rebuilds one using the` title` and` body` alone.` assignees` ,` labels` , and anything GitHub invents later never reach the API because they are never copied. The Slack path does the same with` {channel, text}` , and defuses mention markup in the text itself (` <!channel>` becomes a literal` @channel` , which reads the same to humans but pages nobody).
3. **Operation allowlists.** Only three Slack methods and two GitHub resource shapes are declared. Everything else in those APIs meets a refusal before it’s ever proxied. The gateway functions as an allowlist of operations, not a reverse proxy with rules bolted on.


*An agent can create issues only on repositories in the allowlist.*


## Challenge 4: Agents loop, and loops cost money


**The problem:** An agent stuck retrying a failed call — or deliberately driven into a loop — burns rate limits, backend quotas, and real money on the model side. Ten one-word questions and one enormous document summary share the same call count but result in vastly different bills.


**The counter:** Every proxy inherits a spike arrest and an hourly quota from a shared flow, meaning a looping agent throttles itself without impacting its neighbors. The model plane gets its *own* quota in a separate bucket. This ensures a burst of tool calls won’t exhaust an agent’s ability to think, and a runaway reasoning loop won’t lock it out of its tools.


Because policies are per-identity by construction,` client_id` serves as the throttle key, ensuring a looping agent throttles only itself. Additionally, because the quota limit is read off the API Product at runtime, changing a plan is a simple product edit rather than a proxy redeploy:


```text
<SpikeArrest continueOnError="false" enabled="true" name="SA-SpikeArrest">
<!-- Per-app, not global: one runaway agent must not throttle the others. -->
<Identifier ref="client_id"/>
<Rate>10ps</Rate>
</SpikeArrest>


```


What the throttled caller receives is a sanitized JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) body stripped of Apigee internals and policy names:


```text
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
{"error":"rate_limited","message":"Too many requests too quickly. Slow down and retry."}


HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
{"error":"quota_exceeded","message":"Request quota exhausted for this credential."}


```


*An agent can create issues only on repositories in the allowlist.*


*All throttle and quota events are logged in Cloud Logging.*


## Challenge 5: Unsupervised model requests


**The problem:** Everything above treats the tools as a dangerous surface. But the model call itself is a request to a third party, paid for with a credential, carrying your users’ text. In a standard setup, it’s the only call an agent makes that isn’t seen by any gateway, allowlist, or log.


**The counter:** The example treats the model as one more backend behind the same airlock. The agent’s LLM client points to the gateway’s` /llm/v1` endpoint. Because it’s OpenAI-compatible, any standard client works unmodified, presenting the same consumer key it uses for tools. The gateway enforces protections a provider key never would:


- A model allowlist (an absent allowlist denies every model)
- Deletion of routing fields like` provider` and fallback-model arrays that could bypass the allowlist
- A token ceiling and a refusal of streaming, as Apigee can’t run redaction or auditing over a stream
- A response path that appears secured is *actually not* secure, and there is no clear error.


One identity, two planes, one log. This ensures an agent session is reconstructible rather than a scattered set of unrelated calls.


*An agent can only use models on the allowlist configured in Apigee.*


A refused model call is a first-class audit record. The model named is the exact one the agent asked for. Because a denied request never reaches upstream, the requested name provides crucial context for operators reading the refusal log:


```text
{"ts":"2026-09-01T10:14:02Z", "agent":"agent-reader", "proxy":"llm-v1",
"verb":"POST", "path":"/chat/completions", "action":"llm.chat",
"status":403, "outcome":"denied", "model":"vendor/expensive-model",
"tokens_total":null, "latency_ms":41}


```


*All denied events are logged.*


## Challenge 6: What enters the agent’s context will eventually leave it.


**The problem:** An agent’s context window is a staging area for exfiltration. Every backend response the agent reads — such as a user profile with an email address, an error body with internal details, or an API payload with a credential-shaped field — can be echoed into the next Slack message, GitHub issue, or model prompt the agent produces. And the agent isn’t the only reader. Debug traces and audit logs quietly become a second copy of whatever flowed through the gateway. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) that reaches an agent is PII you no longer control.


**The counter:** Scrub data on the way *out* , at every exit point. Every response, whether it came from a backend or was generated by the gateway itself, passes a redaction pass that drops any key matching` token` ,` secret` ,` password` ,` api_key` , or` authorization` and masks email addresses to` f***@domain` . Every error leaves through a fault sanitizer as one fixed` {"error","message"}` body, so a failure can’t leak Apigee internals or the upstream’s account state either.


Here is what the backend returned versus what the agent actually saw:


```text
// From the backend (a GitHub issue body a human pasted things into):
{"user":{"email":"jane.doe@example.com"},
"body":"contact jane.doe@example.com, deploy key: ghp_a1B2cD34..."}


// What reaches the agent after the redaction pass:
{"user":{"email":"j***@example.com"},
"body":"contact j***@example.com, deploy key: [redacted]"}


```


A matched secret is replaced with a visible marker rather than deleted, deliberately. A silently removed field is indistinguishable from a field that was never there, leaving the model free to invent a plausible value for it. A marker tells the model something was withheld. It also tells whoever reads the audit that this response had a secret in it.


*PII present at the backend — in this case, in a GitHub issue*


*PII never reaches the agent — it’s redacted by Apigee.*


## Challenge 7: You can’t govern what you can’t see.


**The problem:** When something goes wrong with an agent, the first question is, “What did it *try* to do?” A log restricted to successful calls can’t answer that. Worse, most setups have no alerting at all; abuse is discovered when the invoice arrives.


**The counter:** Every request through the gateway, refusals included, writes one JSON record to Cloud Logging. This record includes the agent identity, the action, the outcome, the latency, and (for model calls) the tokens spent. The caller’s key appears only as an eight-character fingerprint, never in spendable form — enough to group one caller’s records together, useless to whoever reads the log.


With one record per request, refusals are recorded exactly like successes, properly identifying the caller:


```text
{
"ts": "2026-08-23T01:27:14.398Z",
"agent": "agent-reader",
"client_key_fp": "4ddfa347",
"proxy": "weather-v1",
"verb": "GET",
"path": "/archive",
"action": "weather.archive",
"status": 403,
"outcome": "denied",
"fault": "InvalidApiKeyForGivenResource",
"latency_ms": 47
}


```


Three alert policies sit on top of the log:


- A burst of write attempts (20 per agent per hour)
- Model` token` spend (2,000 tokens per agent per hour)
- Any denied action at a threshold of zero


No number of allowlist violations per hour is normal.


*Create alerts for what you want to monitor. Legend: MQL = Monitoring Query Language*


*Receive alerts on your medium of choice. This deployment uses Slack.*


## What does all this cost?


The obvious objection is latency. Measured on this deployment, the full chain — including key verification, quota, payload screening, KVM read, credential injection, response redaction, and audit assembly — adds about **90–100 milliseconds** per request. On the model plane, where the upstream itself takes seconds, that overhead is basically noise.


The usual excuse for skipping this layer is, “We can’t put the model behind a gateway; it’s too hot a path.” These measurements prove the opposite.


## Replicate it yourself.


The full example — with proxies, shared flows, provisioning scripts, the MCP server, the ADK agents, and an acceptance suite that proves every claim above with a live test — is available here:


**Deploy it yourself** →[github.com/farooq-kahout-insight/apigee-mcp-gateway](https://github.com/farooq-kahout-insight/apigee-mcp-gateway) — proxies, shared flows, provisioning scripts, the MCP server, the ADK agents, and the smoke-test suite that proves every claim in this post.


To replicate it, you’ll need:


- **A Google Cloud project with an Apigee X organization:** The free evaluation tier is sufficient. You’ll need an environment, an environment group, and an external Application Load Balancer in front of the runtime. The repository’s architecture document maps the exact topology, and` nip.io` provides a resolvable hostname if you don’t own a domain.
- **Local tools:**` bash` , an authenticated` gcloud` ,` apigeecli` ,` python` ,` node` ,` uv` , and` curl` .
- **Credentials to have ready:** A GitHub fine-grained PAT scoped to one repository with Issues read/write, a Slack bot token with` chat:write` and` channels:history` (plus the IDs of the channels you want to allowlist), and an` OpenRouter` API key. The free-tier models are enough for the tests. Each credential goes into the encrypted KVM at provision time and is never committed or logged.


The setup relies on four scripts:` provision.sh` (products, identities, KVMs),` deploy.sh` (proxies and shared flows),` monitoring.sh` (metrics and alarms), and` smoke.sh` .


It’s definitely worth reading the` smoke.sh` acceptance suite. Its tests don’t assert that the gateway works. Instead, they assert that it *refuses* . They verify that a reader can’t` write` , that a non-allowlisted repository is denied without being echoed, and that a refused call still lands in the audit log with the right agent name. A green test run here is evidence, not optimism.


## Ready to test this security pattern?


Explore the open-source repository: Clone the[Apigee MCP Gateway repository](https://github.com/farooq-kahout-insight/apigee-mcp-gateway) to deploy the proxies, MCP server, ADK agents, and automated smoke-test suite.


If you’re running agents against real systems today, pick one of them and ask: What is the worst thing the credential in its environment could do? If the answer makes you uncomfortable, clone the repository, run the smoke suite, and test this pattern against your own backends.
